chapter_text:
CHAPTER 16 - LOCOMOTION AND MOVEMENT

Introduction

All living organisms show movement of one kind or another. A plant bends towards light, the human heart beats without rest, food is pushed along the gut, and a bird flies across the sky. MOVEMENT is one of the defining signs of life. In animals, movement often results in a change of position of the whole body from one place to another - this special kind of movement is called LOCOMOTION. Thus every locomotion is a movement, but not every movement is locomotion. This chapter explains the difference between movement and locomotion, the different types of movement seen in animal cells and bodies, the structure and working of muscles, the human skeletal system that supports the body and provides levers for movement, the joints that make bones move against one another, and finally the common disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems.

16.1 MOVEMENT AND LOCOMOTION

MOVEMENT is any change in the position of a body part or of the whole body. The streaming of cytoplasm inside a cell, the beating of cilia lining our windpipe, the movement of the jaw while chewing, and the pumping of blood by the heart are all examples of movement. LOCOMOTION is the movement of the WHOLE body from one place to another using energy. Walking, running, swimming, flying and crawling are all forms of locomotion. Animals move about in search of food, shelter, a mate, favourable climate, and to escape from enemies or unfavourable conditions.

The methods of locomotion differ from animal to animal. Amoeba uses pseudopodia, Paramecium uses cilia, Euglena uses a flagellum, fish swim with fins, birds fly with wings, and human beings walk and run on two legs. Whatever the method, locomotion requires the coordinated action of the muscular and skeletal systems (together called the LOCOMOTORY or MUSCULOSKELETAL system) along with the nervous system.

16.2 TYPES OF MOVEMENT

Cells of the human body show three main types of movement - amoeboid, ciliary and muscular.

(a) AMOEBOID MOVEMENT: Some specialised cells in our body, such as the white blood cells (leucocytes) and macrophages, move like an Amoeba by forming finger-like projections of the cytoplasm called PSEUDOPODIA (false feet). This movement is brought about by the streaming of cytoplasm and is helped by a network of protein filaments (the cytoskeleton) made of actin. Amoeboid movement helps white blood cells to reach and engulf germs.

(b) CILIARY MOVEMENT: Many internal organs are lined by cells bearing tiny hair-like structures called CILIA. The coordinated beating of these cilia moves substances along a surface. For example, the cilia of the cells lining our respiratory tract (trachea and bronchi) push out dust and mucus, and the cilia in the oviducts (fallopian tubes) move the egg towards the uterus.

(c) FLAGELLAR MOVEMENT: A FLAGELLUM is a long whip-like structure. The movement of the tail of a sperm cell that propels it forward is an example of flagellar movement. Flagella are longer and fewer than cilia but have a similar internal structure.

(d) MUSCULAR MOVEMENT: The movement of our limbs, jaws, tongue and other body parts is brought about by the contraction and relaxation of MUSCLES. Muscular movement is the most important type for locomotion in higher animals, including humans. Muscles can only PULL (contract); they cannot push. Hence they work in opposing pairs (for example the biceps and triceps of the arm) called ANTAGONISTIC muscles.

16.3 MUSCLES AND THEIR TYPES

Muscle tissue is made up of elongated cells called MUSCLE FIBRES that are specialised to contract. Muscle makes up about 40-50 per cent of our body weight. On the basis of their location, structure and function, muscles are of three types.

(a) SKELETAL (STRIATED / STRIPED / VOLUNTARY) MUSCLES: These are attached to the bones of the skeleton by tough cords called TENDONS. Under the microscope they show alternate light and dark bands (striations), so they are called STRIATED muscles. Their cells (fibres) are long, cylindrical, unbranched and MULTINUCLEATE (many nuclei), with the nuclei placed at the edges. Skeletal muscles are under our conscious control, so they are called VOLUNTARY muscles. They are responsible for body movements and locomotion. They contract quickly and powerfully but tire easily (they fatigue).

(b) SMOOTH (UNSTRIATED / VISCERAL / INVOLUNTARY) MUSCLES: These are found in the walls of internal (visceral) organs such as the stomach, intestine, blood vessels, urinary bladder and uterus. Their cells are spindle-shaped (fusiform), unbranched and UNINUCLEATE (a single central nucleus), and they show NO striations. They are NOT under conscious control, so they are INVOLUNTARY. They contract slowly and can stay contracted for a long time without tiring. They carry out functions such as peristalsis (movement of food through the gut).

(c) CARDIAC MUSCLES: These make up the wall of the heart (myocardium). They are STRIATED like skeletal muscle but INVOLUNTARY like smooth muscle. Their cells are branched, uninucleate, and joined end to end at special junctions called INTERCALATED DISCS that allow rapid transmission of impulses. Cardiac muscle contracts rhythmically and tirelessly throughout life without fatigue.

16.4 STRUCTURE OF SKELETAL MUSCLE

A skeletal muscle is a highly organised structure. A whole muscle is made of many bundles called FASCICULI (muscle bundles), each wrapped in connective tissue. Each fasciculus contains many MUSCLE FIBRES (the muscle cells). The cell membrane of a muscle fibre is the SARCOLEMMA, and its cytoplasm is the SARCOPLASM. Each muscle fibre contains many parallel thread-like structures called MYOFIBRILS.

Each myofibril shows a repeating pattern of light and dark bands. The dark bands are called A-bands (Anisotropic) and the light bands are called I-bands (Isotropic). In the middle of each I-band is a dark line called the Z-LINE (or Z-disc). The portion of a myofibril between two successive Z-lines is called a SARCOMERE. The sarcomere is the STRUCTURAL AND FUNCTIONAL UNIT of muscle contraction. In the middle of the A-band is a lighter zone called the H-zone.

Each myofibril contains two kinds of protein filaments (myofilaments):
 - THICK filaments made of the protein MYOSIN, present in the A-band.
 - THIN filaments made of the protein ACTIN, attached to the Z-line and running into the A-band.

Two other proteins, TROPONIN and TROPOMYOSIN, are associated with the actin (thin) filaments and play a key role in controlling contraction. Each thick myosin filament has small projections called CROSS-BRIDGES (myosin heads) that can attach to the actin filaments. The regular, overlapping arrangement of thick and thin filaments gives skeletal muscle its striped (striated) appearance.

16.5 MECHANISM OF MUSCLE CONTRACTION - THE SLIDING FILAMENT THEORY

The way a muscle contracts is explained by the SLIDING FILAMENT THEORY, proposed by A. F. Huxley and H. E. Huxley. According to this theory, muscle contraction occurs when the THIN (actin) filaments SLIDE OVER the THICK (myosin) filaments, so that the two sets of filaments overlap more. The filaments themselves do NOT change in length; they simply slide past each other. As they slide, the Z-lines are pulled closer together, the sarcomere SHORTENS, the I-band and the H-zone become narrower, but the A-band stays the same length. The shortening of all the sarcomeres together shortens the whole muscle - this is contraction.

The steps of contraction are:
1. A nerve impulse (action potential) reaches the muscle fibre at the neuromuscular junction and spreads over the sarcolemma.
2. This causes the release of CALCIUM IONS (Ca2+) from a store inside the muscle called the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm.
3. The calcium ions bind to the protein TROPONIN on the thin filament. This shifts the TROPOMYOSIN and uncovers the binding sites on the actin filament.
4. The myosin heads (cross-bridges) now attach to the exposed sites on actin, forming CROSS-BRIDGES. Using energy from the breakdown of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the myosin heads swivel and PULL the actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere - the power stroke.
5. Fresh ATP binds to the myosin head, which detaches, re-cocks, and attaches to a new site further along - repeating the cycle so the filaments slide further.
6. RELAXATION: When the nerve impulse stops, calcium ions are pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Tropomyosin again covers the binding sites, the cross-bridges break, and the muscle relaxes to its original length.

Thus muscle contraction needs three essentials: CALCIUM IONS (to start the process by exposing the actin sites), ATP (to provide energy for the power stroke and for detachment), and the two contractile proteins ACTIN and MYOSIN. The energy for making ATP comes from the breakdown of glucose. During heavy exercise, when oxygen is short, glucose is broken down by anaerobic respiration to LACTIC ACID, whose build-up causes muscle FATIGUE and cramps.

16.6 THE SKELETAL SYSTEM

The framework of bones and cartilage that supports the body is called the SKELETON. In an adult human it is made of 206 BONES. The skeleton (i) gives SHAPE and SUPPORT to the body, (ii) PROTECTS delicate organs (the skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs), (iii) provides surfaces and LEVERS for the attachment of muscles so that movement is possible, (iv) manufactures BLOOD CELLS in the red bone marrow, and (v) stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.

The human skeleton is divided into two parts: the AXIAL skeleton and the APPENDICULAR skeleton.

(A) AXIAL SKELETON (80 bones): This forms the central axis of the body and consists of the skull, the vertebral column, the ribs and the sternum.
 - SKULL: made of 22 bones - 8 cranial bones that form the brain-box (cranium) and protect the brain, and 14 facial bones. The only movable bone of the skull is the lower jaw (mandible).
 - VERTEBRAL COLUMN (backbone): made of 26 bones called VERTEBRAE. It runs from the base of the skull to the hip and encloses and protects the spinal cord. The vertebrae are grouped into 5 regions: cervical (neck, 7), thoracic (chest, 12), lumbar (lower back, 5), sacral (fused into the sacrum), and coccygeal (fused into the coccyx or tail bone).
 - RIBS: 12 pairs of curved bones that form the RIB CAGE, protecting the heart and lungs. The first 7 pairs (true ribs) join the sternum directly; the next 3 pairs (false ribs) join it indirectly; the last 2 pairs (floating ribs) are not joined to the sternum in front.
 - STERNUM (breast bone): a flat bone in the middle of the chest to which the ribs are attached in front.

(B) APPENDICULAR SKELETON (126 bones): This consists of the bones of the two pairs of LIMBS (arms and legs) and the two GIRDLES that attach the limbs to the axial skeleton.
 - FORELIMB (arm): humerus (upper arm), radius and ulna (forearm), carpals (wrist), metacarpals (palm) and phalanges (fingers).
 - HINDLIMB (leg): femur (thigh - the longest and strongest bone of the body), tibia and fibula (lower leg), patella (kneecap), tarsals (ankle), metatarsals (foot) and phalanges (toes).
 - PECTORAL GIRDLE (shoulder): a pair of clavicles (collar bones) and a pair of scapulae (shoulder blades); it connects the forelimbs to the axial skeleton.
 - PELVIC GIRDLE (hip): formed by two hip bones, each made of three fused bones (ilium, ischium and pubis); it connects the hindlimbs to the axial skeleton and supports the lower body.

16.7 JOINTS

The point at which two or more bones meet is called a JOINT or ARTICULATION. Joints allow movement and hold the skeleton together. On the basis of the amount of movement they permit, joints are of three types.

(a) FIBROUS (FIXED / IMMOVABLE) JOINTS: The bones are held tightly by fibrous connective tissue and allow NO movement. Example: the SUTURES between the bones of the skull.

(b) CARTILAGINOUS (SLIGHTLY MOVABLE) JOINTS: The bones are joined by cartilage and allow only LIMITED movement. Example: the joints between adjacent vertebrae of the backbone and the joint between the two pubic bones (pubic symphysis).

(c) SYNOVIAL (FREELY MOVABLE) JOINTS: These allow FREE movement. The ends of the bones are covered with smooth cartilage, and the joint is enclosed in a capsule filled with SYNOVIAL FLUID that lubricates the joint and reduces friction. Synovial joints are of several kinds:
 - BALL-AND-SOCKET JOINT: the rounded head of one bone fits into the cup-shaped socket of another, allowing movement in ALL directions (rotation). Examples: the shoulder joint and the hip joint.
 - HINGE JOINT: allows movement in ONE plane only, like the hinge of a door (bending and straightening). Examples: the elbow, the knee and the finger joints.
 - PIVOT JOINT: allows ROTATION about an axis. Example: the joint between the first two neck vertebrae (atlas and axis) that lets us turn the head sideways.
 - GLIDING JOINT: flat bone surfaces slide over one another, allowing small sliding movements. Examples: the joints between the wrist (carpal) bones and between the ankle (tarsal) bones.

16.8 DISORDERS OF THE MUSCULAR AND SKELETAL SYSTEM

Several disorders can affect muscles, bones and joints:
 - ARTHRITIS: inflammation of the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. Rheumatoid arthritis is an auto-immune disorder; osteoarthritis is due to wearing away of the joint cartilage with age.
 - OSTEOPOROSIS: an age-related disorder in which the bones become weak, porous and brittle because of loss of bone mass and calcium. It is common in older people, especially women after menopause when the level of the hormone oestrogen falls, and increases the risk of fractures.
 - MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY: a group of INHERITED (genetic) diseases in which the skeletal muscles progressively weaken and waste away (degenerate).
 - TETANY: rapid, painful spasms (twitching) of the muscles caused by a LOW level of calcium ions (Ca2+) in the body fluids, since calcium is needed for normal muscle function.
 - GOUT: painful inflammation and swelling of the joints (often the big toe) caused by the deposition of URIC ACID crystals in the joints due to its excess in the blood.

Taking a balanced diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, exposure to sunlight, and regular exercise help keep the muscles and bones healthy.

SUMMARY

- Movement is any change in the position of a body part; locomotion is the movement of the whole body from one place to another. All locomotion is movement, but not all movement is locomotion.
- Types of movement in the human body: amoeboid (white blood cells, using pseudopodia), ciliary (respiratory tract, oviducts), flagellar (sperm tail) and muscular (limbs, jaw).
- Muscles are of three types: skeletal (striated, voluntary, multinucleate, attached to bones), smooth (unstriated, involuntary, spindle-shaped, in visceral organs) and cardiac (striated, involuntary, branched, with intercalated discs, in the heart).
- A skeletal muscle is made of bundles (fasciculi) of muscle fibres; each fibre contains myofibrils, each divided into sarcomeres (between two Z-lines). Thick myosin filaments and thin actin filaments (with troponin and tropomyosin) give the striated pattern. The sarcomere is the functional unit of contraction.
- Sliding filament theory: actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, sarcomeres shorten, the I-band and H-zone narrow while the A-band stays constant. Contraction needs Ca2+ (to expose actin sites via troponin/tropomyosin), ATP (for the power stroke) and the actin-myosin cross-bridges.
- The human skeleton (206 bones) supports and protects the body, gives levers for movement, makes blood cells and stores minerals. It has an axial part (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and an appendicular part (limb bones and the pectoral and pelvic girdles).
- Joints are fibrous (immovable, e.g. skull sutures), cartilaginous (slightly movable, e.g. between vertebrae) or synovial (freely movable). Synovial joints include ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot (neck) and gliding (wrist) joints.
- Common disorders: arthritis (joint inflammation), osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones), muscular dystrophy (inherited muscle wasting), tetany (spasms from low Ca2+) and gout (uric acid crystals in joints).

topics.description: The organisation of a skeletal muscle into fasciculi, muscle fibres, myofibrils and sarcomeres; sarcolemma and sarcoplasm; A-bands, I-bands, Z-lines and H-zone; thick myosin and thin actin filaments and the proteins troponin and tropomyosin.

chapter_summary.title: Locomotion and Movement - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Biology (314) summary for the Locomotion and Movement lesson. It explains the difference between movement and locomotion, the types of movement and muscle, the structure and working of skeletal muscle (sliding filament theory), the human skeletal system, the types of joints, and the common disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems.

sections.heading: Movement, locomotion and types of movement
bullets: Movement is any change in the position of a body part; locomotion is the movement of the whole body from place to place.
All locomotion is movement, but not all movement is locomotion; animals move for food, shelter, a mate and to escape danger.
Amoeboid movement uses pseudopodia (white blood cells); ciliary movement uses cilia (respiratory tract, oviducts).
Flagellar movement moves the sperm tail; muscular movement moves limbs and jaws and is the basis of locomotion in humans.

sections.heading: Types of muscle
bullets: Skeletal muscle is striated, voluntary, multinucleate and attached to bones by tendons; it moves the body but tires easily.
Smooth (visceral) muscle is unstriated, involuntary, spindle-shaped and uninucleate; it lines internal organs and does not fatigue.
Cardiac muscle forms the heart wall; it is striated but involuntary, branched, with intercalated discs, and never tires.
Muscles can only pull (contract), so they act in antagonistic pairs such as the biceps and triceps.

sections.heading: Skeletal muscle structure and contraction
bullets: A muscle is made of fasciculi of muscle fibres; each fibre contains myofibrils divided into sarcomeres between two Z-lines.
Thick filaments are myosin (A-band); thin filaments are actin (attached to Z-line), with troponin and tropomyosin.
By the sliding filament theory, actin slides over myosin, sarcomeres shorten, and the I-band and H-zone narrow while the A-band stays constant.
Contraction needs Ca2+ (exposes actin sites via troponin/tropomyosin), ATP (energy for the power stroke) and actin-myosin cross-bridges.

sections.heading: The human skeletal system
bullets: The skeleton of 206 bones supports and protects the body, gives levers for movement, makes blood cells and stores minerals.
The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column (26 vertebrae), 12 pairs of ribs and the sternum.
The appendicular skeleton is the bones of the two pairs of limbs plus the pectoral (shoulder) and pelvic (hip) girdles.
The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone; the only movable skull bone is the lower jaw (mandible).

sections.heading: Joints and disorders
bullets: Fibrous joints are immovable (skull sutures); cartilaginous joints are slightly movable (between vertebrae).
Synovial joints are freely movable and contain synovial fluid: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot (neck) and gliding (wrist).
Arthritis is joint inflammation; osteoporosis is weakening of bones from calcium loss, common after menopause.
Muscular dystrophy is inherited muscle wasting; tetany is spasms from low Ca2+; gout is uric-acid crystals in joints.

key_takeaways: Movement is any change of position of a part; locomotion moves the whole body - all locomotion is movement but not the reverse.
The four movement types are amoeboid (WBCs), ciliary (trachea, oviduct), flagellar (sperm) and muscular (limbs).
The three muscle types are skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (unstriated, involuntary) and cardiac (striated, involuntary, heart).
A skeletal muscle runs fasciculus -> fibre -> myofibril -> sarcomere; the sarcomere (between two Z-lines) is the functional unit of contraction.
By the sliding filament theory, actin slides over myosin and sarcomeres shorten; contraction needs Ca2+, ATP, troponin and tropomyosin.
The 206-bone skeleton is axial (skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum) plus appendicular (limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles).
Joints are fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial; common disorders are arthritis, osteoporosis, muscular dystrophy, tetany and gout.

glossary.definition: Any change in the position of a body part or of the whole body, such as the beating of the heart or the bending of a limb.
The movement of the whole body from one place to another, such as walking, swimming or flying, using energy.
Temporary finger-like projections of cytoplasm used for amoeboid movement, as in white blood cells and Amoeba.
Tiny hair-like projections whose coordinated beating moves substances along a surface, as in the respiratory tract.
Striated, voluntary, multinucleate muscle attached to bones by tendons; responsible for body movement and locomotion.
Unstriated, involuntary, spindle-shaped muscle found in the walls of internal (visceral) organs; does not fatigue.
Striated but involuntary branched muscle with intercalated discs, forming the wall of the heart and contracting tirelessly.
The portion of a myofibril between two successive Z-lines; the structural and functional unit of muscle contraction.
The thin (actin) and thick (myosin) contractile protein filaments of muscle whose interaction causes contraction.
The theory that muscle contracts when actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, shortening the sarcomere without the filaments changing length.
The central part of the skeleton - the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum (80 bones).
The bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles that attach the limbs to the axial skeleton (126 bones).
A freely movable joint enclosed in a capsule of lubricating synovial fluid, such as the shoulder, hip, elbow and knee.
An age-related disorder in which bones become weak, porous and brittle from loss of bone mass and calcium.
A painful joint disorder caused by the deposition of uric acid crystals in the joints, often the big toe.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Locomotion and Movement (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer in your own words. Draw and label diagrams wherever helpful. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Distinguish between movement and locomotion, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Movement is any change in the position of a part of the body or of the whole body, without necessarily changing the animal's place - for example, the beating of the heart or the bending of the arm. Locomotion is the movement of the WHOLE body from one place to another using energy - for example, walking, running or swimming. All locomotion is a form of movement, but not all movements are locomotion.
questions.explanation: Definition + one example each; note the whole-body point.

questions.question: Name the four types of movement seen in the human body and give one example of each.
questions.answer: 1. Amoeboid movement - shown by white blood cells (leucocytes) using pseudopodia. 2. Ciliary movement - beating of cilia in the respiratory tract and oviduct. 3. Flagellar movement - movement of the tail of a sperm cell. 4. Muscular movement - movement of the limbs and jaw by contraction of muscles.
questions.explanation: Four types with one example each.

questions.question: Compare skeletal muscle and smooth muscle under three headings: striations, control and location.
questions.answer: Skeletal muscle: it is striated (shows bands), it is voluntary (under conscious control), and it is located attached to the bones of the skeleton. Smooth muscle: it is unstriated (no bands), it is involuntary (not under conscious control), and it is located in the walls of internal (visceral) organs such as the stomach, intestine and blood vessels.
questions.explanation: Three-point contrast: striations, control, location.

questions.question: Define a sarcomere and state why it is important.
questions.answer: A sarcomere is the portion of a myofibril lying between two successive Z-lines (Z-discs). It contains a central A-band (thick myosin filaments) flanked by two half I-bands (thin actin filaments). It is important because it is the structural and functional UNIT of muscle contraction - when sarcomeres shorten, the whole muscle contracts.
questions.explanation: Between two Z-lines; functional unit of contraction.

questions.question: Explain the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction, describing what happens to the bands of the sarcomere and the roles of calcium ions and ATP.
questions.answer:
According to the sliding filament theory (Huxley and Huxley), muscle contraction occurs when the thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments so that they overlap more. The filaments themselves do not shorten; they merely slide past each other.

Steps: (1) A nerve impulse reaches the muscle fibre and causes the release of calcium ions (Ca2+) from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (2) The Ca2+ binds to troponin on the actin filament; this moves tropomyosin and uncovers the binding sites on actin. (3) The myosin heads (cross-bridges) attach to the exposed sites, and using energy from ATP they swivel and pull the actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere (the power stroke). (4) Fresh ATP lets the head detach, re-cock and repeat, so the filaments slide further.

Changes in the sarcomere: the Z-lines are pulled closer, so the sarcomere SHORTENS; the I-band and the H-zone become NARROWER; but the A-band stays the SAME length. When the impulse stops, Ca2+ is pumped back, the sites are re-covered and the muscle relaxes.

Thus Ca2+ starts contraction by exposing the actin sites, and ATP supplies the energy for the power stroke and for detaching the myosin heads.
questions.explanation: Sliding of actin over myosin; I-band/H-zone shorten, A-band constant; Ca2+ exposes sites, ATP powers stroke.

questions.question: List any four functions of the human skeletal system.
questions.answer: 1. It gives shape and support to the body. 2. It protects delicate internal organs (the skull protects the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs). 3. It provides levers and surfaces for the attachment of muscles, making movement possible. 4. It manufactures blood cells in the red bone marrow and stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.
questions.explanation: Support, protection, movement/levers, blood formation/mineral storage.

questions.question: Distinguish between the axial and appendicular skeleton, naming the main bones of each.
questions.answer: The axial skeleton forms the central axis of the body and consists of the skull, the vertebral column (backbone), the ribs and the sternum (breast bone); it has 80 bones. The appendicular skeleton consists of the bones of the two pairs of limbs (arm bones such as humerus, radius, ulna; leg bones such as femur, tibia, fibula) together with the pectoral (shoulder) and pelvic (hip) girdles that attach the limbs to the axial skeleton; it has 126 bones.
questions.explanation: Axial = skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum; appendicular = limbs + girdles.

questions.question: Name the three types of joints on the basis of movement and give one example of each.
questions.answer: 1. Fibrous (fixed / immovable) joint - allows no movement; example: the sutures between the bones of the skull. 2. Cartilaginous (slightly movable) joint - allows limited movement; example: the joints between adjacent vertebrae of the backbone. 3. Synovial (freely movable) joint - allows free movement; example: the shoulder or knee joint.
questions.explanation: Fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial with examples.

questions.question: Describe the four types of synovial joints, giving one example and the kind of movement each allows.
questions.answer:
Synovial joints are freely movable joints lubricated by synovial fluid. They are of four main kinds:

1. Ball-and-socket joint: the rounded head of one bone fits into the cup-shaped socket of another and allows movement in all directions (rotation). Examples: the shoulder joint and the hip joint.

2. Hinge joint: allows movement in one plane only (bending and straightening), like a door hinge. Examples: the elbow, the knee and the finger joints.

3. Pivot joint: allows rotation about an axis. Example: the joint between the first two neck vertebrae (atlas and axis) that lets us turn the head sideways.

4. Gliding joint: flat bone surfaces slide over one another, allowing small sliding movements. Examples: the joints between the wrist (carpal) bones and the ankle (tarsal) bones.
questions.explanation: Ball-socket (all directions), hinge (one plane), pivot (rotation), gliding (sliding), with examples.

questions.question: What is osteoporosis? Why is it common in older women, and how does it affect the bones?
questions.answer: Osteoporosis is an age-related disorder in which the bones lose mass and calcium and become weak, porous and brittle, so they break easily. It is common in older women, especially after menopause, because the level of the hormone oestrogen falls and bone loss speeds up. As a result the bones become fragile and the risk of fractures increases. A diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, sunlight and regular exercise help to prevent it.
questions.explanation: Weak porous bones from calcium/bone loss; post-menopause oestrogen fall; higher fracture risk.

questions.question: Give two reasons why animals move from one place to another.
questions.answer: Animals move about (i) in search of food, water, shelter and a mate, and (ii) to escape from enemies (predators) or from unfavourable conditions such as extreme heat, cold or lack of oxygen.
questions.explanation: Two reasons: obtaining resources; escaping danger/unfavourable conditions.

questions.question: Describe amoeboid movement and state where it occurs in the human body.
questions.answer: In amoeboid movement a cell forms temporary finger-like projections of its cytoplasm called pseudopodia (false feet) and flows into them, so the cell creeps along, just like an Amoeba. It is brought about by the streaming of cytoplasm helped by a network of protein (actin) filaments. In the human body it is shown by white blood cells (leucocytes) and macrophages, which use it to reach and engulf germs.
questions.explanation: Pseudopodia + cytoplasmic streaming; occurs in white blood cells.

questions.question: Where does ciliary movement occur in the human body? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Ciliary movement occurs where cells bear tiny hair-like cilia. Two examples are: (i) the lining of the respiratory tract (trachea and bronchi), where cilia sweep out dust and mucus, and (ii) the oviducts (fallopian tubes), where cilia move the egg towards the uterus.
questions.explanation: Respiratory tract and oviduct.

questions.question: Compare skeletal and cardiac muscle under the headings striations and control.
questions.answer: Striations: both skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated (they show light and dark bands). Control: skeletal muscle is voluntary (under conscious control), whereas cardiac muscle is involuntary (it beats on its own, not under conscious control). Cardiac muscle is also branched with intercalated discs and does not fatigue, while skeletal muscle is unbranched and tires easily.
questions.explanation: Both striated; skeletal voluntary, cardiac involuntary.

questions.question: Give two features of smooth muscle.
questions.answer: Smooth muscle (i) is unstriated (shows no bands) and its cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus, and (ii) is involuntary and found in the walls of internal organs such as the stomach, intestine and blood vessels, where it contracts slowly without tiring.
questions.explanation: Two of: unstriated, spindle-shaped, uninucleate, involuntary, visceral, fatigue-resistant.

questions.question: Why do muscles work in antagonistic pairs? Illustrate with the arm.
questions.answer: A muscle can only pull (contract); it cannot push itself back to its original length. So to produce movement in two opposite directions, muscles are arranged in opposing (antagonistic) pairs. In the arm, when the biceps (in front of the upper arm) contracts, it bends (flexes) the arm at the elbow; to straighten the arm again the triceps (behind the upper arm) contracts while the biceps relaxes. Thus the two muscles act antagonistically to bend and straighten the arm.
questions.explanation: Muscles only pull; biceps flexes, triceps extends the arm.

questions.question: Describe the organisation of a skeletal muscle from the whole muscle down to the myofibril.
questions.answer: A whole skeletal muscle is made of many bundles called fasciculi, each wrapped in connective tissue. Each fasciculus contains many muscle fibres, which are the muscle cells (long, cylindrical and multinucleate). The cell membrane of a fibre is the sarcolemma and its cytoplasm is the sarcoplasm. Inside each fibre are many parallel thread-like myofibrils, which are divided along their length into repeating units called sarcomeres.
questions.explanation: Muscle -> fasciculus -> fibre -> myofibril (-> sarcomere).

questions.question: Name the two contractile proteins of a myofibril and state which forms the thick and which the thin filament.
questions.answer: The two contractile proteins are myosin and actin. Myosin forms the thick filaments (found in the A-band), and actin forms the thin filaments (attached to the Z-line). Two regulatory proteins, troponin and tropomyosin, are also present on the thin (actin) filament.
questions.explanation: Myosin = thick; actin = thin.

questions.question: What are the A-band, I-band and Z-line of a myofibril?
questions.answer: In a myofibril the dark band is the A-band (anisotropic), which contains the thick myosin filaments; the light band is the I-band (isotropic), which contains only thin actin filaments. Running through the middle of each I-band is a dark line called the Z-line (Z-disc), to which the thin filaments are attached. The region between two successive Z-lines is one sarcomere.
questions.explanation: A-band dark (myosin); I-band light (actin only); Z-line in mid I-band anchors actin.

questions.question: State the role of calcium ions in muscle contraction.
questions.answer: When a nerve impulse reaches a muscle fibre, calcium ions (Ca2+) are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm. The Ca2+ ions bind to the protein troponin on the thin filament; this shifts the tropomyosin and uncovers the binding sites on actin. The myosin heads can then attach to actin and pull it, causing contraction. Thus calcium ions trigger contraction by exposing the actin binding sites. When Ca2+ is pumped back, the muscle relaxes.
questions.explanation: Ca2+ binds troponin -> tropomyosin shifts -> actin sites exposed -> contraction.

questions.question: What happens to the I-band and the A-band when a muscle contracts?
questions.answer: When a muscle contracts, the thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments and the Z-lines are pulled closer. As a result the I-band (which contains only actin) becomes NARROWER (shortens), while the A-band (the length of the myosin) stays the SAME. The H-zone also narrows.
questions.explanation: I-band shortens; A-band unchanged.

questions.question: Why does a muscle become fatigued during vigorous exercise?
questions.answer: During vigorous exercise the muscle needs a lot of energy (ATP), which is normally made by breaking down glucose using oxygen. When exercise is heavy, oxygen supply may fall short, so the muscle breaks down glucose by anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid. The build-up of lactic acid in the muscle causes the feeling of tiredness, pain and cramps known as muscle fatigue. After rest, oxygen removes the lactic acid and the muscle recovers.
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration -> lactic acid build-up -> fatigue.

questions.question: Name the four parts of the axial skeleton.
questions.answer: The axial skeleton consists of (i) the skull, (ii) the vertebral column (backbone), (iii) the ribs, and (iv) the sternum (breast bone).
questions.explanation: Skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum.

questions.question: How does the skeleton protect the internal organs? Give two examples.
questions.answer: The skeleton forms hard, bony cases around delicate organs. For example, (i) the skull (cranium) forms a strong box that protects the brain, and (ii) the rib cage, formed by the ribs, sternum and thoracic vertebrae, protects the heart and lungs. The vertebral column also encloses and protects the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Cranium protects brain; rib cage protects heart and lungs.

questions.question: Describe the arrangement of ribs in the human rib cage.
questions.answer: There are 12 pairs of ribs. The first 7 pairs are called true ribs and join the sternum directly by cartilage. The next 3 pairs are false ribs and join the sternum indirectly. The last 2 pairs are floating ribs and are not attached to the sternum in front. Together they form the rib cage that protects the heart and lungs.
questions.explanation: 7 true, 3 false, 2 floating pairs.

questions.question: Name the bones of the human forelimb (arm).
questions.answer: The bones of the forelimb are: the humerus (upper arm); the radius and ulna (forearm); the carpals (wrist); the metacarpals (palm); and the phalanges (finger bones).
questions.explanation: Humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges.

questions.question: What is the pelvic girdle and what is its function?
questions.answer: The pelvic girdle (hip girdle) is formed by two hip bones, each made of three fused bones - the ilium, ischium and pubis. It joins the hindlimbs (legs) to the axial skeleton, supports the weight of the upper body, and protects the lower abdominal organs such as the urinary bladder and reproductive organs.
questions.explanation: Two hip bones (ilium+ischium+pubis); attaches legs and supports the body.

questions.question: Name the bones that make up the pectoral girdle.
questions.answer: The pectoral (shoulder) girdle is made up of a pair of clavicles (collar bones) and a pair of scapulae (shoulder blades). It connects the forelimbs (arms) to the axial skeleton.
questions.explanation: Clavicles and scapulae.

questions.question: What is a synovial joint? How is it suited for free movement?
questions.answer: A synovial joint is a freely movable joint. In it the ends of the bones are covered with smooth cartilage, and the joint is enclosed in a capsule filled with synovial fluid. The smooth cartilage and the lubricating synovial fluid reduce friction between the bones, and the loose capsule allows the bones to move freely against each other. Examples are the shoulder, hip, elbow and knee joints.
questions.explanation: Cartilage + synovial fluid reduce friction, allowing free movement.

questions.question: Give one example each of a fibrous and a cartilaginous joint.
questions.answer: A fibrous (immovable) joint is found between the bones of the skull (the sutures). A cartilaginous (slightly movable) joint is found between the adjacent vertebrae of the backbone (and at the pubic symphysis between the two pubic bones).
questions.explanation: Fibrous: skull sutures; cartilaginous: between vertebrae.

questions.question: What is arthritis? Name its two common forms.
questions.answer: Arthritis is the inflammation of the joints, which causes pain, swelling and stiffness and makes movement difficult. Its two common forms are: (i) rheumatoid arthritis, an auto-immune disorder in which the body attacks its own joints, and (ii) osteoarthritis, in which the cartilage of the joint wears away with age.
questions.explanation: Joint inflammation; rheumatoid (auto-immune) and osteoarthritis (wear of cartilage).

questions.question: What is muscular dystrophy?
questions.answer: Muscular dystrophy is the name for a group of inherited (genetic) diseases in which the skeletal muscles progressively become weak and waste away (degenerate). The affected person gradually loses muscle strength and the ability to move.
questions.explanation: Inherited disease with progressive weakening and wasting of muscles.

questions.question: Describe the four types of movement seen in the human body, giving the mechanism and an example of each.
questions.answer:
The human body shows four main types of movement:

1. Amoeboid movement: certain cells such as white blood cells and macrophages form finger-like projections of cytoplasm called pseudopodia and flow into them, creeping along like an Amoeba. It is helped by the streaming of cytoplasm and actin filaments. Example: white blood cells moving to engulf germs.

2. Ciliary movement: cells bearing tiny hair-like cilia beat them in a coordinated way to move substances along a surface. Example: cilia of the trachea sweep out dust and mucus; cilia of the oviduct move the egg.

3. Flagellar movement: a long whip-like flagellum lashes to and fro to propel a cell. Example: the beating tail of a sperm that drives it forward.

4. Muscular movement: the contraction and relaxation of muscles moves body parts. Example: movement of the limbs, jaw and tongue. Muscular movement is the basis of locomotion in humans.
questions.explanation: Amoeboid (pseudopodia/WBC), ciliary (cilia/trachea), flagellar (sperm), muscular (limbs).

questions.question: Compare the three types of muscle - skeletal, smooth and cardiac - with respect to location, structure, control and fatigue.
questions.answer:
Skeletal (striated) muscle: located attached to the bones of the skeleton; its fibres are long, cylindrical, unbranched and multinucleate and show striations; it is voluntary (under conscious control); it contracts fast and powerfully but fatigues quickly. It brings about body movement and locomotion.

Smooth (unstriated / visceral) muscle: located in the walls of internal organs such as the stomach, intestine, blood vessels and bladder; its cells are spindle-shaped, unbranched and uninucleate and show no striations; it is involuntary; it contracts slowly and does not tire. It carries out functions such as peristalsis.

Cardiac muscle: located in the wall of the heart; its cells are striated, branched and uninucleate and are joined by intercalated discs; it is involuntary; it contracts rhythmically throughout life without fatigue.

Thus skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary, smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary, and cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary and never tires.
questions.explanation: Location, cell shape/nuclei/striations, control and fatigue for each of the three muscle types.

questions.question: With the help of the parts of a sarcomere, describe the detailed structure of a myofibril.
questions.answer:
A myofibril is a fine thread inside a muscle fibre and is made of repeating units called sarcomeres. A sarcomere is the region between two successive Z-lines (Z-discs).

Each myofibril shows a pattern of light and dark bands. The dark band is the A-band (anisotropic), which contains the thick filaments made of the protein myosin. The light band is the I-band (isotropic), which contains only the thin filaments made of the protein actin. Each thin filament is attached to a Z-line that runs through the middle of the I-band. In the centre of the A-band is a lighter region called the H-zone, where only myosin is present.

The thin (actin) filaments also carry two regulatory proteins, troponin and tropomyosin. The thick (myosin) filaments bear small projections called cross-bridges (myosin heads) that can attach to actin. The regular overlapping arrangement of thick and thin filaments gives the myofibril, and hence skeletal muscle, its striated appearance. The sarcomere is the structural and functional unit of contraction.
questions.explanation: Sarcomere between Z-lines; A-band (myosin), I-band (actin), H-zone; troponin/tropomyosin; cross-bridges.

questions.question: Explain, step by step, the mechanism of muscle contraction according to the sliding filament theory, and describe how the muscle relaxes.
questions.answer:
By the sliding filament theory (Huxley and Huxley), a muscle contracts when the thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments, without either filament changing length.

Steps of contraction: (1) A nerve impulse reaches the muscle fibre at the neuromuscular junction and spreads over the sarcolemma. (2) This causes calcium ions (Ca2+) to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm. (3) The Ca2+ binds to troponin on the thin filament, which moves the tropomyosin aside and uncovers the binding sites on actin. (4) The myosin heads (cross-bridges) attach to these exposed sites; using energy from the breakdown of ATP, they swivel and pull the actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere - the power stroke. (5) Fresh ATP binds the myosin head, which detaches, re-cocks and attaches to a new site further along, repeating the cycle so the filaments slide further.

As a result the Z-lines are pulled closer, the sarcomere shortens, and the I-band and H-zone narrow while the A-band stays the same; the whole muscle contracts.

Relaxation: when the impulse stops, calcium ions are pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, tropomyosin again covers the actin sites, the cross-bridges break, and the muscle returns to its original relaxed length.
questions.explanation: Impulse -> Ca2+ release -> troponin/tropomyosin shift -> cross-bridge power stroke (ATP) -> sarcomere shortens; relaxation reverses via Ca2+ re-uptake.

questions.question: Describe the axial skeleton of the human body and the functions of the skeleton.
questions.answer:
The axial skeleton forms the central axis of the body and has 80 bones in four parts:
1. Skull: made of 22 bones - 8 cranial bones forming the brain-box that protects the brain, and 14 facial bones; the only movable bone is the lower jaw (mandible).
2. Vertebral column (backbone): 26 vertebrae running from the skull to the hip, enclosing and protecting the spinal cord; grouped into cervical (7), thoracic (12), lumbar (5), sacral (sacrum) and coccygeal (coccyx) regions.
3. Ribs: 12 pairs of curved bones forming the rib cage that protects the heart and lungs.
4. Sternum: the flat breast bone in the middle of the chest to which the ribs join in front.

Functions of the skeleton: (i) it gives shape and support to the body; (ii) it protects delicate organs (skull -> brain, ribs -> heart and lungs); (iii) it provides levers and surfaces for muscle attachment, making movement possible; (iv) it makes blood cells in the red bone marrow; and (v) it stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.
questions.explanation: Skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum; five functions of the skeleton.

questions.question: Describe the appendicular skeleton, naming the limb bones and the two girdles.
questions.answer:
The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) consists of the bones of the two pairs of limbs together with the two girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton.

Forelimb (arm): humerus (upper arm); radius and ulna (forearm); carpals (wrist); metacarpals (palm); phalanges (fingers).

Hindlimb (leg): femur (thigh - the longest and strongest bone); tibia and fibula (lower leg); patella (kneecap); tarsals (ankle); metatarsals (foot); phalanges (toes).

Pectoral (shoulder) girdle: a pair of clavicles (collar bones) and a pair of scapulae (shoulder blades); it attaches the forelimbs to the axial skeleton.

Pelvic (hip) girdle: two hip bones, each formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis; it attaches the hindlimbs to the axial skeleton and supports the lower body.

Thus the appendicular skeleton provides the limbs for movement and the girdles that anchor them to the body.
questions.explanation: Arm bones, leg bones, pectoral girdle (clavicle+scapula), pelvic girdle (ilium+ischium+pubis).

questions.question: Classify joints on the basis of movement and describe each type with examples.
questions.answer:
On the basis of the amount of movement they allow, joints are of three types:

1. Fibrous (fixed / immovable) joints: the bones are held tightly by fibrous tissue and allow no movement. Example: the sutures between the bones of the skull.

2. Cartilaginous (slightly movable) joints: the bones are joined by cartilage and allow only limited movement. Example: the joints between adjacent vertebrae, and the pubic symphysis.

3. Synovial (freely movable) joints: the bone ends are covered with cartilage and the joint is enclosed in a capsule of lubricating synovial fluid, allowing free movement. They are of several kinds:
 - Ball-and-socket joint - movement in all directions; e.g. shoulder and hip.
 - Hinge joint - movement in one plane only; e.g. elbow, knee, fingers.
 - Pivot joint - rotation about an axis; e.g. between the atlas and axis vertebrae (turning the head).
 - Gliding joint - small sliding movements; e.g. between the wrist (carpal) bones.

Thus joints range from completely fixed to freely movable, matching the needs of different parts of the body.
questions.explanation: Fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial (ball-socket, hinge, pivot, gliding) with examples.

questions.question: Describe five common disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems and their causes.
questions.answer:
1. Arthritis: inflammation of the joints causing pain, swelling and stiffness; it may be rheumatoid arthritis (an auto-immune disorder) or osteoarthritis (wearing away of joint cartilage with age).

2. Osteoporosis: an age-related disorder in which the bones lose mass and calcium and become weak, porous and brittle, so they fracture easily; it is common in older women after menopause because of a fall in oestrogen.

3. Muscular dystrophy: a group of inherited (genetic) diseases in which the skeletal muscles progressively weaken and waste away.

4. Tetany: rapid, painful spasms (twitching) of the muscles caused by a low level of calcium ions in the body fluids, since calcium is needed for normal muscle function.

5. Gout: painful inflammation and swelling of the joints (often the big toe) caused by the deposition of uric acid crystals due to excess uric acid in the blood.

A balanced diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, exposure to sunlight and regular exercise help to keep the muscles and bones healthy.
questions.explanation: Arthritis, osteoporosis, muscular dystrophy, tetany, gout with causes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Rahul watched a documentary. He saw an Amoeba creeping by pushing out lobes of cytoplasm, a fish swimming with its fins, and a close-up of a human sperm lashing its long tail. He also learnt that the cells lining our windpipe are covered with tiny beating hairs that push out dust.
(a) Name the type of movement shown by the Amoeba and the structures it uses.
(b) What is the difference between the movement of the fish and that of a beating heart?
(c) Name the type of movement shown by the sperm tail and by the hairs of the windpipe.
questions.answer:
(a) The Amoeba shows amoeboid movement, using temporary projections of cytoplasm called pseudopodia (false feet).
(b) The fish swimming is locomotion, because the whole body moves from one place to another. The beating of the heart is only a movement, because a body part moves without the whole body changing place. So all locomotion is movement, but not all movement is locomotion.
(c) The sperm tail shows flagellar movement (the tail is a flagellum); the beating hairs of the windpipe show ciliary movement (the hairs are cilia).
questions.explanation: Tests amoeboid vs ciliary vs flagellar movement and the movement/locomotion distinction.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student examined three muscle tissues under a microscope. Tissue X had long, cylindrical, unbranched fibres with many nuclei and clear stripes. Tissue Y had spindle-shaped cells with a single nucleus and no stripes. Tissue Z had branched, striped cells joined end to end by special discs.
(a) Identify tissues X, Y and Z.
(b) State whether each is voluntary or involuntary.
(c) Give one location in the body for each tissue.
questions.answer:
(a) X is skeletal (striated) muscle; Y is smooth (unstriated / visceral) muscle; Z is cardiac muscle (the discs are intercalated discs).
(b) X (skeletal) is voluntary; Y (smooth) is involuntary; Z (cardiac) is involuntary.
(c) X is found attached to bones (e.g. the biceps of the arm); Y is found in the walls of internal organs (e.g. the stomach or intestine); Z is found only in the wall of the heart.
questions.explanation: Identifies the three muscle types by structure, control and location.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Under a powerful microscope a myofibril shows alternating dark and light bands. A dark line runs through the middle of each light band. The region between two of these dark lines is described as the working unit of the muscle. Two kinds of protein filaments, one thick and one thin, lie side by side.
(a) Name the dark band, the light band and the dark line.
(b) What is the region between two dark lines called, and why is it important?
(c) Name the proteins that make the thick and the thin filaments.
questions.answer:
(a) The dark band is the A-band, the light band is the I-band, and the dark line running through the I-band is the Z-line.
(b) The region between two successive Z-lines is the sarcomere. It is important because it is the structural and functional unit of muscle contraction - when sarcomeres shorten, the muscle contracts.
(c) The thick filaments are made of myosin and the thin filaments are made of actin.
questions.explanation: Tests the bands of the myofibril, the sarcomere and the filament proteins.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
During a race an athlete's leg muscles contract repeatedly. Inside each muscle fibre, calcium ions are released, protein filaments slide past one another, and ATP is used up. Near the end of the race the athlete's muscles begin to ache and feel tired.
(a) From where are the calcium ions released, and what do they do?
(b) Which filaments slide over which, and what happens to the sarcomere?
(c) Explain why the athlete's muscles ache and feel tired.
questions.answer:
(a) Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum inside the muscle fibre. They bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin aside and uncovers the binding sites on actin, allowing contraction to begin.
(b) The thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments. As a result the Z-lines are pulled closer and the sarcomere shortens (the I-band and H-zone narrow while the A-band stays the same).
(c) During hard exercise the muscles run short of oxygen, so glucose is broken down anaerobically to lactic acid. The build-up of lactic acid causes the aching, tiredness and cramps known as muscle fatigue.
questions.explanation: Applies Ca2+ role, sliding filament changes and lactic-acid fatigue to exercise.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A teacher told the class that muscle contraction needs three things: a trigger ion, a protein that responds to it, and an energy source. Without any one of them, the muscle cannot contract.
(a) Name the trigger ion and the protein it binds to.
(b) Name the energy source and say what it is used for.
(c) What happens to this ion when the muscle relaxes?
questions.answer:
(a) The trigger ion is calcium (Ca2+); it binds to the protein troponin on the thin (actin) filament.
(b) The energy source is ATP (adenosine triphosphate). Its energy is used by the myosin heads for the power stroke (pulling the actin) and for detaching the heads so the cycle can repeat.
(c) When the muscle relaxes, the calcium ions are pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum; tropomyosin then covers the actin sites again and the muscle returns to rest.
questions.explanation: Tests Ca2+/troponin, ATP role and Ca2+ re-uptake during relaxation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The human skeleton is often divided into two parts. One part forms the central axis of the body and protects the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs. The framework is also a factory for blood cells and a store of minerals.
(a) Name the part of the skeleton that forms the central axis and list its four components.
(b) Which structures protect the brain and which protect the heart and lungs?
(c) State two other functions of the skeleton mentioned in the passage.
questions.answer:
(a) The central axis is the axial skeleton. Its four components are the skull, the vertebral column, the ribs and the sternum.
(b) The skull (cranium) protects the brain; the rib cage (ribs with the sternum) protects the heart and lungs. The vertebral column protects the spinal cord.
(c) Two other functions: it makes blood cells in the red bone marrow, and it stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.
questions.explanation: Tests the axial skeleton, protection of organs and blood/mineral functions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In an accident a cyclist broke the long bone of his thigh and also injured his shoulder region, where the collar bone and shoulder blade meet the arm. The doctor explained which parts of the appendicular skeleton were affected.
(a) Name the thigh bone that was broken and state one fact about it.
(b) Name the two bones of the shoulder (pectoral) girdle.
(c) To which part of the skeleton - axial or appendicular - do these bones belong?
questions.answer:
(a) The thigh bone is the femur. It is the longest and strongest bone of the human body.
(b) The two bones of the pectoral (shoulder) girdle are the clavicle (collar bone) and the scapula (shoulder blade).
(c) All these bones - the femur, clavicle and scapula - belong to the appendicular skeleton (the limbs and their girdles).
questions.explanation: Applies knowledge of the femur, pectoral girdle and appendicular skeleton.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
While playing, Meera could rotate her arm at the shoulder in a full circle, bend her arm only in one direction at the elbow, and turn her head from side to side. She noticed her skull bones, however, did not move at all.
(a) Name the type of joint at the shoulder and the type at the elbow.
(b) Which joint allows her to turn her head sideways?
(c) Why do the bones of the skull not move?
questions.answer:
(a) The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint (allows movement in all directions); the elbow is a hinge joint (allows movement in one plane only).
(b) The head is turned sideways at the pivot joint between the first two neck vertebrae (the atlas and axis).
(c) The bones of the skull are joined by fibrous (fixed / immovable) joints called sutures, so they cannot move.
questions.explanation: Distinguishes ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot and fibrous joints from everyday movements.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
An elderly woman complained of frequent bone fractures. Her doctor said her bones had become weak and porous after menopause. Her neighbour, an older man, had a swollen, painful big toe caused by crystals deposited in the joint.
(a) Name the woman's bone disorder and give its cause.
(b) Why is this disorder common after menopause?
(c) Name the man's joint disorder and the substance whose crystals cause it.
questions.answer:
(a) The woman has osteoporosis, caused by loss of bone mass and calcium, which makes the bones weak, porous and brittle so they fracture easily.
(b) It is common after menopause because the level of the hormone oestrogen falls, which speeds up the loss of bone mass.
(c) The man has gout, caused by the deposition of crystals of uric acid in the joint.
questions.explanation: Tests osteoporosis (cause, menopause link) and gout (uric acid crystals).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Three patients visit a clinic. Patient A has painful muscle twitches; a blood test shows very low calcium. Patient B has swollen, stiff and painful joints. Patient C, a young boy, is slowly losing muscle strength, and the doctor says it is an inherited condition affecting several boys in the family.
(a) Name the disorder of Patient A and its cause.
(b) Name the general disorder of Patient B.
(c) Name the disorder of Patient C and state why it runs in the family.
questions.answer:
(a) Patient A has tetany, caused by a low level of calcium ions in the body fluids, which leads to painful muscle spasms.
(b) Patient B has arthritis (inflammation of the joints), which causes swelling, stiffness and pain.
(c) Patient C has muscular dystrophy. It runs in the family because it is an inherited (genetic) disorder passed from parents to children, so several members can be affected.
questions.explanation: Differentiates tetany, arthritis and muscular dystrophy from clinical clues.
